inline.s: The song says:
O plank-back fellow, plank-back man, how sorely has he swindled you, and spun his plan!
You long for lightness on your back, and heed not how your feet may crack.
Even bore you it to before your birth, it long has cloaked the half of all your earth.
This very plank, this pillory at the neck, your every bone and flesh it does subject.
If you do not at once throw it down, a hundred thousand kalpas' foe it will be your own.
Sitting it's a burden, walking too, a clear impediment—why not see it through?
Only because you once mistook it so, within a pure and quiet gate a demon you let grow.
Eyes open, eyes closed, it is still seen; in broad day the vast void shoots lightning between.
A gandharva city floats where nothing stands; the fool mistakes it for heaven's palace-lands.
To gain the light, you must let it fall; a rank dead toad—what price at all?
Black beans are offered for your eyes so bright; mark well the fish-eye from the pearl aright.
There is one road, the best to tread, straight and open as a balance spread.
But do not by the flowers and willows stay, and you shall reach the emperor's seat that day.
Cast off your body and your life, like earth outspread; the ox, the horse, the camel, ass you need not dread.
If you can fling it past Mount Sumeru's height, sword-trees and knife-hills are a child's delight.
If you love it, by it you are beset; the burden swells with all the tending and the fret.
Break once the crystal bottle, and it is done— the great earth, mountains, rivers all are gone.
I counsel you, sir: do not bear the load; the very skull its sweat sheds on that road—and dries at once, as you let go.
Split your body, scatter form in countless kinds, and from this day the gate of death you shall not find.

Reading the Song of the Plank-Bearing Fellow, its vivid words so full of wisdom make clear the landscape along the Chan path and the tidings of reaching home; it is truly a guide to the real practice of the Chan school.

blocks.text: 22. The Bodhisattva Appears in the World

inline.s: In the forty-fifth year of the Wanli reign (

), the Master was seventy-two. In the first month, after taking leave of the assembly at Jingshan, he went to Yunqi Mountain to mourn the Master of Yunqi. More than a thousand of the Yunqi Master's disciples had long awaited him in the mountain. In the meditation hall the Master disclosed to the assembly the hidden practices of the Yunqi Master in life; as they listened, some wept and sobbed aloud. They asked the Master to compose the Stupa Inscription for Master Yunqi Lianchi Hong (
see further
Annotated Stupa Inscription of Master Lianchi
essay

When the Master left the mountain, the Dharma Master Xuanjin, the layman Tan Mengxun, and many Confucian scholars and gentlemen urged him to expound the Bodhisattva precepts at Jingsi Temple. At that time the Master wrote a Record of the Zongjing Hall
(Record of the Zongjing Hall of Jingsi Temple by West Lake)

The news that the Master was in Hangzhou drew many renown 'ed worthies from across the land, who gathered at West Lake; each set forth his views and posed challenges, and the Master answered every one. The atmosphere was most warm, and the assembly a magnificent Dharma gathering such as the southeastern region had never seen.

Here, the Dharma Master Xuanjin and the layman Tan Mengxun gathered the scattered works the Master had composed during his earlier wanderings and published them as the Collected Works of the Eastern Journey.

By now the Master's practice had grown daily more consummate. Though he spread the Dharma everywhere, he never needed a whisk or a monk's staff at hand. His countenance was bright as jade, and his body very strong; even walking in the bitter heat he had not a drop of sweat. Morning and evening, when he washed, the water in the basin remained clear and never muddy. When he sat he always took the full lotus posture, and it needed no help from his hands. Closing his eyes he entered samadhi, and opening them he left it; whether at the roadside or by lamplight, walking, standing, sitting, or lying, it was ever so. By day or by night, in walking, standing, sitting, or lying, at the first sound of another's request for the Dharma he would open his eyes with brilliance like lightning. There was no trace of any matter in his eyes, nor need to wipe them. When he ascended the hall to expound the Dharma, his eloquence was unimpeded; at the first word he would produce hundreds or thousands of characters without ever stumbling, and his voice boomed like a great bell, shaking all beyond the hall. When he took up his brush to write words of instruction, without rising from his seat he would set down hundreds or thousands of characters, never pausing. Ordinarily his left hand turned the prayer beads unceasingly, while his right held a folding fan of white bamboo ribs, in his hand winter and summer alike, lifted without a wave and closed without opening. Whenever he had to command some great matter touching the three worlds of gods and men, a single strike on the table rang true.

The Master's spiritual powers and supernormal abilities manifested themselves without number. One day when he was at the Zongjing Hall, having ascended the hall to expound the Dharma, he saw two monks escorting a third up the steps, while the one being escorted raved without ceasing. The two monks begged the Master, saying, “This elder brother has recited the Great Compassion Mantra for five years and has always been upright in behavior; we do not know why he has become possessed like this. We beg the Master to cure him.” The Master said, “This illness can be cured!” He bade his attendant seek out in the hall three monks who held the Vajra mantra of the impure and glorious one. First, from his seat the Master himself held the mantra, then had the three monks pass it to the raving monk. At first the man was unconscious. With a single majestic strike of his fan upon the table, the Master would utter a line, and the mad monk could follow and hold it; when the whole mantra had been imparted line by line, the raving monk awoke as from a dream and at once returned to normal.

On another day a monk came to bow. Before he had finished, the Master struck the fan and shouted, “Murderous thief, why have you come to see me?!” The guest-master monk heard and hurried over, but the bowing monk left without a word. The assembly stared in stunned bewilderment. The next day the monk was arrested by the authorities, and only then did the assembly understand the Master's wondrous powers.

The Master's supernatural deeds are too many to enumerate. Once, when he was in the meditation hall of Jinming Temple at Jiaxing, discussing the Dharma with friends in the evening, suddenly a man holding a club began shouting outside the hall door. Some recognized him as the runner Qian of the grain office, and, taking him for drunk, wanted to drive him off. But instead of leaving he shouted the louder, and his cries were mixed with Buddhist terms: “A living bodhisattva has come today; I should be delivered from the path of rebirth! Do not stop me.” The company found this strange and reported it. The Master said, “Let him come in.” As the man entered, he joined his palms and bowed, bearing the dignified bearing of a child of the Buddha. The assembly watched in curiosity as he knelt and said, “This disciple is Zhong Riren. In life I kept a long fast and cultivated the Pure Land for eight years. Today is the thirty-fifth day of my demise, and I have borrowed the body of the runner Qian to beg the Master to deliver me. I do not wish to go to the underworld; I want to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. I pray the bodhisattva to guide me with compassion.” Having spoken, he bowed his head to the ground and wept without pause. The Master bade six elders among his attendants who specialized in Pure Land practice to stand by, and himself turned the prayer beads; then he had them give the man a set of beads and recite the name of the Buddha a thousand times, and the body that hosted the soul could follow in the recitation, the whole hall silent in solemn stillness. When the recitation was done, the Master again lectured on the text of the Mengshan food-bestowal rite, and as he intoned, “One should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm—all is created by the mind alone,” he struck the table with his fan and cried out, “Be swiftly released!” The man answered, “I am released!” This was repeated three times, three calls and three answers, with utmost speed. Then the body that had hosted the soul arose, with the dignified bearing of a Buddha-child, and thanked the Master for attaining rebirth in the Pure Land. It bowed to the assembly on both sides, saying, “Each of you strive on—we shall meet at the Dragon-Flower Assembly!” The assembly were still gathered in the hall, not yet dispersed; some wept, some sighed, some laughed secretly, and some even murmured in blame; the Master was unmoved and met all with equanimity. The man followed the crowd to see the Master off to his boat by the river, gratefully bowing to him, then returned to the hall door, spoke a few words thanking the elder Qian for lending his body for the deliverance, and suddenly fell to the ground and woke as the runner Qian once more. At this, a knowing bystander said, “Zhong Riren was the father of the scholar Zhong across the river; in life he cultivated the Pure Land with utmost devotion, so such a response was only fitting.” The Master's newly converted lay disciple Fu Zheng, standing by, said, “The scholar Zhong is my friend Zhong Shengfu.” Thereupon they went with a dozen or more fellow believers to visit the household, and only then learned that Zhong Riren had died thirty-five days before, and that the runner Qian, having come to his spirit-table on account of grain collection, had been used by Zhong Riren, who seized the moment of his drunkenness to gain deliverance.

A few days later, a layman named Xu Taiwei, who had long believed in the Buddha, having witnessed the Master's supernatural powers, invited him to his home to hold a memorial for his father, and begged the Master to speak the Dharma. In a single discourse the Master pointed out every hidden misdeed of the father during his lifetime, and all who heard were awed by the Master's astonishing spiritual power.

In only a few days the news spread from mouth to mouth that a living bodhisattva had appeared in the world. Men, women, young, and old alike, each with a heart of devotion, wished to see the Master. At that time the Master was at the East Pagoda, and in a moment the crowds came swarming; tens of thousands filled every space from the mountain gate to the abbot's chamber, and the cries of those who wished to see him swelled on and on. Then the Master, with a few attendants, walked to the window on the second storey of the East Pagoda and greeted the assembly with compassion. At the sight of the Master the worshippers rose and fell in waves, like clouds piled upon clouds. From the Master's virtue and supernormal powers they saw the greatness of Buddhism, and their devotion and joy within were beyond words. They kept on bowing until dark, and only then gradually dispersed.

The next day the tide of people coming to worship and make offerings to the Master still surged without ceasing. Feeling that it was wrong to let things continue thus, on the third day the Master crossed the river to Songling.

[Editor's note] The original events above are found in the Commentary on the Chronicle of Master Hanshan, and were witnessed by Fu Zheng, the author of the Commentary and a disciple of Master Hanshan. The Commentary says:
“Zheng
(Fu Zheng)
followed
(the Master's)
spiritual power and supernormal abilities, witnessing a hundred such manifestations; I shall record their chief features briefly.”

blocks.text: 23. Pointing All Back to the Pure Land

inline.s: In the forty-sixth year of the Wanli reign (

), the Master was seventy-three. That year he began to build a Buddha hall and a meditation hall at Wuru Temple. Emulating the admirable precedent of Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, who chanted the Buddha's name through the six divisions of the day, he marked the hours with incense in place of the water-clock, and told the disciples to have images of the Three Holy Ones of the Western Land exquisitely made in the Buddha hall.

[Wuru Temple] lies south of Mount Lu beneath the five-peaked summit, and is also called Wuru Monastery. It was first founded in the Song dynasty. When Master Hanshan came here from Caoxi, he took a liking to the landscape and enlarged and rebuilt the temple. After the expansion it rose in fame, and its incense flourished, with pilgrims and visitors coming without cease. The temple enshrines the portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs of Buddhism, a masterpiece of the artist Ding Yunpeng of Xin'an, with a record by the Jingling-school poet Tan Yuanchun.

The following year, after the halls were completed, the Master began reciting the Avatamsaka Sutra in the first month; during this period he also expounded the Comprehensive Discussion of the Lotus Sutra for the assembly. In the summer he further explained for them the Surangama Sutra, the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana, the Diamond Sutra, the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, and the Treatise on Consciousness-Only, among others.

On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the Dharma assembly of sutra lectures being complete, the Master entered a retreat, shutting himself off from all outside engagements. In his quiet room he marked the hours by incense in place of the water-clock, and through the six periods
(twelve hours)
he chanted the Buddha's name, devoting himself wholly to the Pure Land.
[Marking the hours by incense, chanting through the six periods, devoted to the Pure Land] In a letter Replying to the Grand Secretary Qian Shouzhi, Master Hanshan wrote:
“In my present retreat
(in the closed retreat)
I have set aside completely all matters of Chan and the Dharma, and simply hold to my plainness
(that is, single-mindedly chanting the Buddha's name; holding to plainness here means no longer investigating Chan or prying into doctrine)
I especially emulate the Venerable Yuan's lotus water-clock of the six periods
(the 'lotus water-clock' was a device by which Huiyao, a disciple of Master Huiyuan, marked time at the Lu-shan monastery by making the lotus flower serve as the clock)
, using incense in place of the flower
(I burn incense to mark time in place of the lotus water-clock)
. For these months past,
my body and mind have of themselves reached supreme bliss
Dream-Wandering Collection

Before long, the Master further considered that the Avatamsaka school was about to be lost, since the commentaries of Master Qingliang were vast in wording and broad in meaning, and scholars, unable to command them, mostly dared not go deep. Taking only the essential purport of the commentary, the Master set pen and wrote the Compendium of the Avatamsaka, which played a part in the revival of that school.
In the forty-eighth year of the Wanli reign (

), the Master was seventy-five. That spring, his attendant Guangyi asked him to write a Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, a Direct Explanation of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, and a Commentary on the Seven Inner Chapters of Zhuangzi.

In the summer the Master developed a foot ailment and could not walk easily. In the autumn many lay practitioners came up the mountain to ask about the Way; though ill, the Master gave them instruction on the Dharma, and also composed more than seventy brief biographies of the successive patriarchs, each with an appended eulogy, which he put into circulation.

It had been eight years since the Master left Caoxi for Mount Lu, and the disciples dwelling at Caoxi longed for him day and night. They often sent representatives to Mount Lu to inquire, wishing to invite the Master back, but he declined every time. Later many lay practitioners of Caoxi also came to invite him, and the Master, pleading illness, gently refused their earnestness.

The following summer the disciples asked the Master to explain the Notes on the Surangama. In the tenth month, his disciple, the provincial graduate Liu Qixiang, and others again invited him to Caoxi, and again the Master declined on the ground of illness.
In the second year of the Tianqi reign (

), the Master was seventy-seven. That year he completed the Compendium of the Avatamsaka, and again explained for the assembly the Surangama Sutra, the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, and the Treatise of Master Zhao. At this time many disciples, including the prefect Wu of Caoxi and the prefect of Shaoyang, urged the Master for a third time to go to Caoxi; unable to refuse, he resolved to make the journey. That winter the Master left Mount Lu, crossed Peng Lake, and on the eighth day of the twelfth month climbed to the lands south of the ridge; on the fifteenth he entered Caoxi. There, at the request of the assembly, he began to write his chronicle.
In the third year of the Tianqi reign (

), the Master was seventy-eight. In the spring, the prefect of Shaoyang and other lay practitioners came into the mountain to ask the Master to speak the Dharma, and disciples such as Faxing of Wuyang also arrived at Caoxi. Though aged, the Master, with the bodhisattva's compassionate heart, gave the gift of the Dharma without weariness: at the meditation hall he first conferred the great precepts on the assembly, then spoke on the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, the Treatise on Consciousness-Only, and the Surangama Sutra.

In the eighth month the Master sent an attendant to thank the prefect Wu for the sincerity of his protection of the Dharma. As the attendant was about to set out, the Master said, “In spreading the Dharma, the Buddhas and patriarchs prize the right occasion and conditions; when conditions run against the time, on what shall teaching rely? This period's work is done—I am about to return!” The assembly heard this in bewilderment, thinking the Master wished to return to Mount Lu.

On the Double Ninth Festival the Master wrote for his attendant Shengguang the Poem of Dwelling in the Mountains, and in his colophon said, “Though this old man is lazy with the brush and inkstone, I fear that if the breath does not come again, I shall be making a debt to the next life. If you regard these as mere poems and words, then you slight my kindness much!”

On the first day of the tenth month, the disciple Tong Jiong came from Mount Lu to pay his respects; the Master asked in detail after the resident congregation of Wuru Temple and the elders of the mountain monasteries, and was very pleased. Then the disciple Jingtai asked the Master to compose a “self-eulogy” setting out the great outlines of his life.

On the third day of the tenth month, the junior minister (vice-minister of the Personnel Board) Xiao Xuanpu came into the mountain to visit the Master. The Master talked with him through three days and nights; when the minister begged him for the essentials of the Dharma, the Master at once wrote out two teachings and three poems for him.

On the sixth the minister left the mountain. The Master admonished him, “On you rest the hopes of the state and its people; take care on the road ahead!” When the minister set a time to meet again, the Master said, “This mountain monk is old, and the four elements are about to part; when you and I meet again, it shall be at the Dragon-Flower Assembly!”
[Dragon-Flower Assembly]

Maitreya Bodhisattva now dwells in the inner court of the Tusita Heaven; in the future he will descend to the world and become a Buddha, holding an assembly beneath the Dragon-Flower tree in the Hualin Garden to deliver gods and humans alike—this is called the “Dragon-Flower Assembly.”
On the eighth, the Master showed a slight ailment; the disciples and congregation came to ask after him, and the Master said to them, “The old man is just weary, not ill!”

On the ninth, the disciples brought medicine to the Master, who said, “I am about to depart—of what use is medicine to me!” His attendant Guangyi, greatly startled, cried, “If the Master should pass away
(a euphemism for death)

, what last instruction have you to leave?” The Master rebuked him: “You have served this old man for many years—how can you hold such an understanding?” Then he said to the assembly, “You must remember that the matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift; make earnest Buddha-recitation!” Guangyi asked again, “If the Master does not utter a single word, what shall we follow?” The Master said, “What was proclaimed by the golden mouth has become old paper already; of what use are my words?” And so he left not a single word.

On the twelfth day of the tenth month, the Master's birthday, monks and lay disciples gathered at Caoxi. The prefect of Shaoyang came into the mountain to offer a purple gauze meditation robe as a birthday gift, and the two sat face to face in talk through the whole day. At night, after the prefect had gone, the Master called for water and bathed. The next morning he put on the purple gauze robe the prefect had given and went to take leave of him. When the prefect again came to the Master's bed, the Master said, “This mountain monk is going now; many thanks for the great protector's kind heart!” The prefect said, “The Master's Dharma-body is well; I,
(a humble way of referring to oneself)
guard this land and am its host, so all is in my care.” Upon hearing this, the Master smiled, joined his palms, and gave thanks.

At noon the prefect took leave and descended the mountain. The Master at once had his attendant bring clean water for rinsing the mouth, and said, “Today I cut the tangled vine.” He then had his attendant bring hot water for a bath and a change of clothes. Afterward he gathered the assembly to sit around him and chant the Buddha's name. When the chanting ceased, the Master said to them, “Do not be alarmed. Follow the Buddha's statutes: you must not wear the hempen mourning garments, and you must not wail. Set your minds on a single-hearted Buddha-recitation!”
At the hour of Shen
(three to five in the afternoon)

, the eye of gods and men, the guide of the three worlds, sat upright and passed away. That night a light of down made the sky bright; the birds of the mountain sang in lament, and the cries of grief of the monastic and lay disciples shook the valleys.
After the Master's nirvana, his countenance remained as white and smooth as jade, his lips still so ruddy, his hands and feet still so soft, just as when he entered samadhi.
[Editor's note] In his latter years Master Hanshan practiced Buddha-recitation in seclusion at the five-peaked summit of Mount Lu, and in the Dream-Wandering Collection
Autobiographical Chronicle he wrote:
“In the forty-seventh year, the year ji-wei, I was seventy-four.
On the full moon of the eighth month
(the fifteenth day of the eighth month)
I entered a retreat, cutting off all conditions, emulating the Venerable Yuan
(Master Huiyuan, first patriarch of the Pure Land school)
, and through the six periods
(twelve hours)
marked the hours by incense in place of the water-clock,
devoting myself wholly to the Pure Land karma
In a letter Replying to the Grand Secretary Qian Shouzhi, he wrote:
“In my present retreat
(in the closed retreat)
I have set aside completely all matters of Chan and the Dharma, and simply hold to my plainness
(that is, single-mindedly chanting the Buddha's name; holding to plainness here means no longer investigating Chan or prying into doctrine)
I especially emulate the Venerable Yuan's lotus water-clock of the six periods
(the 'lotus water-clock' was a device by which Huiyao, a disciple of Master Huiyuan, marked time at the Lu-shan monastery by making the lotus flower serve as the clock)
, using incense in place of the flower
(I burn incense to mark time in place of the lotus water-clock)
. For these months past,
my body and mind have of themselves reached supreme bliss
(Collected from the Dream-Wandering Collection)
Master Hanshan passed into nirvana on the thirteenth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Tianqi reign (
), at the age of seventy-eight. According to the Commentary on the Chronicle of Master Hanshan:
On the twelfth, the Master's birth anniversary
(his birthday)

, monastic and lay disciples gathered. The prefect of Shaoyang, Lord Zhang Sanxing, came into the mountain to present a purple gauze meditation robe for the monk's longevity, and the two sat talking together through the whole day. In the evening, Lord Zhang departed. That very night the Master called three times for water for his bath.

The next morning he at once called for the meditation robe Lord Zhang had sent, put it on, and went to take leave of him. When Lord Zhang again came to his bed, the Master said, 'This mountain monk is going; many thanks for the great protector's kind heart.' Lord Zhang said, 'The Master's Dharma-body is well; I,
(a humble self-referring phrase meaning 'this unworthy one')
guard this land and am its host, so all is in my care.' The Master smiled, joined his palms, and gave thanks.
At noon
the thirteenth day of the tenth month
at midday)

, after Lord Zhang had departed, he at once bade his attendant bring clean water to rinse his mouth, saying, 'Today I cut the tangled vine.' Then he called for hot water for a bath and a change of clothes,
and the assembly sat around chanting the Buddha's name
. He admonished them, 'You must not be alarmed; follow the Buddha's statutes, do not wear the hempen mourning garments, and do not wail,
but set your minds on single-hearted Buddha-recitation
Exactly at the hour of Shen
(three o'clock in the afternoon)

, the Master sat upright and passed away. That night a light of down lit up the sky, the birds lamented, and the cries of the monastic and lay disciples shook the valleys. After he had gone, he sat upright for three days, his face pale, his lips ruddy, his hands and feet soft, as though he had entered dhyana.
This shows that Master Hanshan, through Buddha-recitation, was reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Master Hanshan not only practiced Buddha-recitation himself and sought rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, but strongly maintained that all approaches should be directed toward the Pure Land. In the Preface Directing All to the Pure Land in the Dream-Wandering Collection
, the Master wrote:
“If
the Pure Land approach
, it embraces all three capacities, sudden and gradual alike enter it, and no faculty is left unencompassed—what is called the horizontal transcendence of the three worlds:
this is the supreme approach
Among the patriarchs of old and those who awakened to mind, there has not been one who did not take this as his final refuge
, such as Nagarjuna
(Bodhisattva Nagarjuna)
and Asvaghosa
(Bodhisattva Asvaghosa)
who praised it with utmost effort.
.” “For those of the highest faculties in Chan,
there is none who does not return to the Pure Land
Five days before entering stillness, he admonished his attendant:
“You must bear in mind that the matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift;
make earnest Buddha-recitation
(Commentary on the Chronicle of Master Hanshan)
The Master's disciples sent word to the prefect, who at once dispatched an official to come mourn and to seal the Master's reliquary for him.

The junior minister Xiao Xuanpu, who had left the Master only five days before and was still at Xiongzhou, on hearing of his passing mourned through the whole day. But when he learned of the circumstances of the Master's final moments, he was greatly rejoiced and said, “The Master was a man of the sage's station; had he not been utterly thorough at the gate of birth-and-death, how could he have been so free and at ease?” He at once composed an elegy and dispatched it in mourning. He also donated two hundred pieces of gold and wrote a letter charging the two prefects of Nan and Shao to build a portrait hall for the Master.

The disciples at Wuru Temple on Mount Lu, hearing of the Master's passing, at once hurried to Caoxi. On the twenty-first day of the first month they escorted the Master's reliquary back to Wuru, arriving at Fayun Temple on the five-peaked summit of Kuang Mountain on the twenty-eighth day of the second month.

After the disciples escorted the Master's body to Mount Lu, since the climate there was damp and humid, the attendant Fushan built a pagoda court and placed the Master's body-shrine within the pagoda.

Eleven years later, fierce tigers roamed Mount Lu and Fayun Temple on the five-peaked summit was in danger. Fearing the pagoda ground was unsafe, Fushan respectfully brought out the Master's body-shrine; seeing that half of the protecting shrine had been eaten away by insects and ants, he dared not bury it, and so sealed it again in the pagoda as before.

Nine more years passed, and the Lingnan disciples Chen Zongbo, Liu Qixiang, and others, entrusted by the Buddhist community of Caoxi, went to Mount Lu to welcome the Master back to Caoxi. When the Master's body was being escorted to Meiling, they chanced to meet the newly appointed governor-general of Guangdong
(another term for the regional commander)
Song Zhaoming, who had his soldiers carry the shrine in a cart and personally escorted it to Caoxi.

Only a few months after taking office, Song Zhaoming again came to Caoxi. The disciples guarding the shrine, Guangcheng and Cili, seeing a crack in the shrine chamber, secretly bored a little hole in it and peered through. They beheld the Master's body seated upright as if alive; they wished to open the shrine but could not make up their minds. When Song Zhaoming learned of this, he drew his sword and split open the crack. There they saw the Master seated in the lotus posture, as majestic as in life; his nails and hair were still growing, his complexion still fresh and ruddy, his robes and shoes as new. At that moment a gust of wind arose, and the garments suddenly scattered like clouds and stars, fluttering away with it; the people of the district gathered them up as tokens of auspiciousness.
Just then a monk suddenly arrived, asking leave to use the Indian
(ancient India)
method to protect the Master's body. Once the assembly agreed, he took sandalwood powder from Hainan and painted the Master's body as though with lacquer. When he had done, he went off by himself.

While the Master was alive, a devout girl of Caoxi, who had made a vow to embroider a robe of a thousand Buddhas to offer to him, fearing her breath not clean, wrapped her mouth in a yellow silk cloth as she worked. By the time the robe of a thousand Buddhas was finished, the Master had already entered the shrine, and the robe was stored in the treasury of Baolin. Now they took it out again and draped it on the Master's body; though twenty years had passed, it shone with color as if newly made. The disciples placed the Master's body in the old pagoda court for veneration, calling it Hanshan Temple, about half a li from Nanhua Temple, where the body of the Sixth Patriarch dwells.

[Editor's note] The Commentary on the Chronicle of Master Hanshan says: the above events were recorded in person by Guangcheng and Ciren. Guangcheng was the abbot of Fayun Temple, and Ciren the abbot of Qixia Temple; they were the Dharma-disciples and personal attendants who, on the two journeys of welcoming and escorting the shrine, went to and from Caoxi. Guangcheng was a personally transmitted disciple of Master Hanshan, and Ciren was Guangcheng's disciple. The Commentary records:
“The teacher Xuzhong, named Guangyi, at the Baolin assembly
(the meditation session that Master Hanshan led in the Baolin hall of Nanhua Temple at Caoxi)
, personally realized nirvana.
The teacher Xuzhong had a disciple Ciren, styled Jianru, who was abbot of Qixia.”

In accordance with the custom of making offerings to the Sixth Patriarch, the disciples each morning used a basin of hot fragrant water to steam the Master's face until it sweated, then wiped it dry with a cloth, and thereafter offered food and drink as in life. Once a year they also bathed him.

Each year, in the second and eighth months, Buddhist disciples from across the land came in bands up the mountain to pay homage to the body of Master Hanshan; with hearts of utmost reverence they bowed and made vows before him, drawing strength of spirit for seeking the Buddha-way above and saving sentient beings below. Today, more than four hundred years later, the Master still sits there in his firm, indestructible diamond body. Who says the Master has passed away? Does he not still with those compassionate eyes watch over the world and benefit all sentient beings?
